title.en: The Jackal Sets Lion Cub and Tiger Cub at Variance

region.en: Forest of Kalasuta (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 迦臘須多林（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXIII B, The Jackal as Calumniator (Kah-gyur vi. 239-243)

summary.en: A lioness adopts a tiger cub and a tigress a lion cub; the mothers charge the two foster-brothers, named Sudanshthra and Subahu, never to listen to calumniators. An old remainder-devouring jackal, finding the tiger the rival of his maw, tells each that the other plans to kill him, warning each to fear the other's stretching, yawning, triple roar. When the two notice for the first time these natural gestures, each draws the wrong conclusion - and then both speak slokas, ask 'who told you?', discover the jackal, and strike him dead.
summary.zh: 母獅收養虎崽，母虎收養獅崽；二獸臨終囑咐兄弟倆勿聽讒言。一隻食殘的老豺見虎為爭食之敵，便向彼此謊稱對方欲害己，並預言對方伸腰、呵欠、三嘯即殺機。兩獸初次注意到這些本性舉止，便誤信讒言——隨後雙方對誦偈語，互問「是誰告訴你的」，揪出豺狼，一掌擊斃。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: A tigress, finding a stray lion cub, made it a playfellow for her own and suckled it; the lioness returning cried out 'sister, run not away - let us dwell together, so that when I go out you can take care of my young one, and when you go out, I will take care of yours.' The cubs were named Sudanshthra the lion and Subahu the tiger, and when the mothers lay dying they charged the pair: as ye have both sucked the same dugs, be brothers; the world is full of evil calumniators - take heed not to listen to any of them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal as Calumniator (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: An old, remainder-devouring jackal followed the lion, and saw in the tiger the antagonist of his maw. He came with drooping ears and told the lion that the tiger had vowed to kill him, then told the tiger the lion had vowed the same - adding to each the prophecy of the fatal gestures: he will stretch himself, and yawn, and look round on all four sides, and roar three times, and then come into your presence and think, 'he will kill me.' Be sure of that.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal as Calumniator (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The day came when lion and tiger each did exactly what the jackal had described - gestures they had made all their lives without once noticing them. Now the seed of discord was sown: each thought the other meant murder. But the lion reflected that he was strong and the tiger not, and investigated; both recited slokas avowing no strife, asked who had spoken, and learned the truth. The lion struck the jackal dead with a slap, and a deity sang that friends must not be abandoned for others' words but the words tested - no reliance on calumniators.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal as Calumniator (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Otters and the Jackal Mukhara

region.en: River bank, Kah-gyur narrative India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河岸（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXIV, The Two Otters and the Jackal (Kah-gyur ff. 94-95)

summary.en: Two otters agree to fish together, one driving fish ashore, the other killing them; neither dares divide the catch for fear of unrighteous division, so the jackal Mukhara undertakes it. He belittles each otter's share of the work, then divides the heap into heads, tails and middles, assigning tails to the land-otter, heads to the water-otter - and the middle parts to himself, 'he who is conversant with the law.' He carries the choicest middle of a great fish home to his rejoicing mother.
summary.zh: 雙獺合力捕魚，一驅魚上岸，一殺魚；均懼分贓不公而互讓。豺摩訶羅自請主分，先貶低各獺之功，再把魚堆分為頭、尾、中三份——尾歸陸獺，頭歸水獺，中段「歸曉法者」，自己取走大魚最肥的中段，回家向母親炫耀。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Two otters resolved that one should go into the water and frighten the fish ashore while the other killed them, sharing the spoil in common. When the heap of fish was great, each begged the other to divide it, both fearing to make a mistake in a righteous division. The jackal Mukhara, coming up, undertook the task - first questioning each otter's contribution and overawing them both, so that they sat heart-smitten and silent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Two Otters and the Jackal (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mukhara divided the heap into three parts - heads, tails, and the rest of the bodies - and uttered his verse: 'The goer on land receives the tails, and the goer into the depths the heads; he who is conversant with the law receives the middle parts.' Seizing the middle part of a large fish, he went off to his mother, who joyfully hailed him: 'O Mukhara, fine and fair exceedingly art thou who hast been too much for the otters; they twain are content, and thou hast secured a rich booty.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Two Otters and the Jackal (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jackal Rescues the Lion from the Well

region.en: Hill district with an old well (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 有古井的山地（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXV, The Jackal Saves the Lion (Kah-gyur iv. 244)

summary.en: The Bodhisattva, born as a lion, feeds five hundred jackals on his leavings; hunting by night he falls into a well, and all the jackals scatter but one, who studies how to draw him out. Digging a canal from a nearby lake, he fills the well with water until the lion floats free - 'the mighty as well as the rest must make themselves friends.'
summary.zh: 菩薩生為獅王，以獵物殘餘養五百豺；夜獵落井，群豺四散，唯有一豺留而設法——在旁掘渠引湖水灌井，使獅浮起得脫。「強者亦須交友。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The lion, king of beasts, killed animals and left them lying for the jackals; hunting beasts at night he fell into a well, and all the five hundred jackals dispersed except one, who sat by the edge thinking how he could draw the lion out. Running to and fro, he saw a small lake, dug a canal on one side, and filled the well with water from the lake, so that the lion was able to get out. A deity sang: the mighty as well as the rest must make themselves friends - see how the jackal rescued the lion from an old well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal Saves the Lion (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Dyer's house and forest edge (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 染坊與林緣（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXVI, The Blue Jackal (Kah-gyur iv. 255)

summary.en: A greedy jackal falls into an indigo vat, rolls on a dunghill, and comes out a colour never seen before; proclaimed Sataga, king of the fourfooted beasts by Sakra, he rides an elephant with lions in the inner circle and jackals far outside. His mother, invited, notes the wrong ordering and sings that so long as he utters no jackal's cry his prosperity holds - but nature defeats him: hearing his own kind howl, he must howl or lose his hair, and the elephant beneath him, hearing the cry, flings him down and tramples him.
summary.zh: 貪吃的豺跌入靛缸、滾過糞堆、入水曬日，得一身從未見過的顏色；自稱天帝釋所立的四足獸王「薩多伽」，騎象而立，獅虎在內圈，豺群在外圈。其母受邀，嘆息秩序顛倒，唱言「只要他不發豺聲，大象便容他享福」——然而本性難違：不嗥則毛落，他一開口，座下大象知是豺而將他摔落踐斃。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: A very greedy jackal fell into an indigo vat in a dyer's house, rolled on a dunghill, jumped into water, and came out with the colour of cyanite. The other jackals stood afar and asked who he was; he answered that he was Sataga, appointed king of the fourfooted beasts by Sakra, and the awed beasts made him their king - the inner circle lions and tigers, the outer jackals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Blue Jackal (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He sent for his mother from her mountain ravine, and the messenger jackal reported that the inner circle was lions and elephants but the outer jackals. 'So much for things not following their proper order,' she said, singing that so long as he utters no jackal's cry the elephant will let him retain his prosperity. But when the jackals howled round him, he knew that if he kept silent his hair would fall off - so, sitting on the elephant, he lifted up his voice; the elephant flung him off and trampled him under foot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Blue Jackal (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jackal Hanged by the Ox

region.en: Lotus swamp of a hill-town (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山鎮蓮塘（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXVII, The Jackal Hanged by the Ox (Kah-gyur iv. 293)

summary.en: An ox of signs, stuck in a swamp, asks its owner to throw it a noose and go; if a jackal comes, it will pick up the noose with its horns and throw it over him. The jackal, sure of a feast, refuses warning; the ox invites him to mount its back for food - and slings the noose round his neck, leaving him dancing in the air with verses about dancing-masters and ladders to Brahma's world.
summary.zh: 帶相之牛陷於沼澤，請主人拋繩而去，並言若有豺來，便以角挑繩套之。貪食的豺不聽警告，牛誘其上背覓食，隨即用角甩繩套其頸，令其懸空「起舞」——雙方以「舞師」與「天梯」互相唱和。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The householder flung a noose before the ox and went away; by night up came a jackal asking who tore up the lotus roots and white lotuses. Warned of harm and disgrace, the jackal still prepared to injure the ox, who offered verse-bait: 'No lotus roots do I tear up... if thou wishest for food mount upon my back, there wilt thou find food.' Gluttony carried the jackal onto the ox's back, the ox flung the noose with its horn, caught him round the neck, and let him hang in the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal Hanged by the Ox (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In mid-air the two traded verses: 'Art thou Jakara the dancing-master?' mocked the ox; 'Sakara has provided a ladder, I betake myself to Brahma's world,' answered the jackal; and the ox closed the contest: 'Sakara has not provided a ladder; as thou hast been laid in the fetters of contrivance, thou wilt never see thyself saved.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal Hanged by the Ox (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Jackal in the Elephant's Footprints

region.en: Water-hole in the Himalayan foothills (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山麓水塘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXVIII, The Jackal in the Elephant's Footprints (Kah-gyur iv. 222)

summary.en: Following an elephant to drink, a jackal begins to measure its own stride against the great footprints and claims them for its own; springing forward it sets a foot in one and trips over a broken piece of kandakilaka wood - 'thy footprints and those of the elephant are not alike; give up this useless attempt.'
summary.zh: 豺隨象至水邊，以己步量象跡，妄稱跡為己有；一躍踏跡，絆於斷木而跌——「爾之跡與象跡不同，莫作無益之試。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: An elephant came to the Himalayas to drink, and in its track followed a jackal which began to measure its own stride with the great footprints, saying to itself, 'these footprints are mine.' Springing forward it set its foot in one and tripped over a broken piece of wood. A deity sang: in a word, fool, thy footprints and those of the elephant are not alike; give up this useless attempt - thou wilt only derive weariness therefrom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Jackal in the Elephant's Footprints (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Guilty Dogs and the Hair-Pellet

region.zh: 波羅奈梵授王馬廄（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXXIX, The Guilty Dogs (Kah-gyur iv. 212)

summary.en: Two dogs, Ganda and Upaganda, have gnawed the king's horse-gear to pieces; as he takes the field against the Licchavis the sabotage is found, and all the dogs of the court are slaughtered or put to flight. A stranger dog, finding them terrified, offers to implore the king for them, and the whole pack recite a verse of protest from a distance. The king demands a test: the dogs are given a hair-pellet and made to vomit - and only Ganda and Upaganda bring up leather, so all the rest are freed from fear.
summary.zh: 伽達與優波伽達二犬啃壞王的馬具；出征前發覺，犬群或被殺或逃。一外鄉犬替眾犬向王哀求，群犬隔遠合唱抗辯之偈。王令驗證：以毛丸令眾犬嘔吐——唯二犬吐出皮革碎片，於是被處死，其餘免於恐懼。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Some dogs were killed and others ran away; a dog from another country, seeing them in flight, asked what had frightened them, and on hearing the story said: why do you not implore the king? - we who run away have no power to implore, they answered, and the others have been rendered mute. Wait awhile, said the stranger, I will implore the king in your behalf; and after a halt the pack expressed their prayer in a verse: these two dogs full of force and health ought to be put to death; we are not deserving of death - it is not right to let the innocent be put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Guilty Dogs (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The ministers, ordered to find out whether the horse-gear was devoured by Ganda and Upaganda or by other dogs, could think of only one way: the dogs must be given a hair-pellet and made to vomit. Given and made to vomit, Ganda and Upaganda brought up fragments of leather; the king delivered them to death and rendered all the others free from fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Guilty Dogs (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Mouse-hole beside a thicket (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 叢邊鼠穴（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XL, The Hypocritical Cat (Kah-gyur iv. 247-248)

summary.en: Aging out of the hunt, the cat Agnija takes to performing fictitious acts of penance beside the mouse-hole, declaring that he atones for the sins of his youth. The five hundred mice, nourished on faith, run their rounds in confidence - and every day the cat devours the one that comes last. The mice-chief, watching his troop dwindle as the cat grows sleek, observes the trick, and pronounces his verse: this is not a genuine penance but one performed only for the sake of gain - because the number of the mice diminished have you, Agnija, thrived.
summary.zh: 老貓阿耆尼惹捕鼠無力，便在鼠穴旁佯作苦行，自稱懺悔青年時代的罪業。五百小鼠滿懷信心出入，而每日末位之鼠總被吞。鼠王見族減而貓肥，窺破其計，隔遠誦偈：「此非真苦行，乃為口腹而修行——鼠數日減，汝阿耆尼惹日肥。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The cat took to performing fictitious acts of penance at a spot not far from the mouse-hole, and when the mice asked what he was doing he answered that he was making up for many vicious actions of his youth. Confidence grew in the troop; but as they returned to their hole after every round, the cat seized and devoured the mouse which came last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Hypocritical Cat (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seeing the troop dwindle while the cat thrived fat and well covered with hair, the mice-chief watched from a hiding-place, saw the trick, and pronounced his verse: he who eats roots and berries will not become fat - this is not a genuine penance but one performed only for the sake of gain; because the number of the mice diminished have you, Agnija, thrived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Hypocritical Cat (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Gazelle Prince and the Faithful Doe

region.en: Netted glade of a hill forest (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山林網套之地（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLI, The Gazelle and the Hunter (Kah-gyur iv. 244-245)

summary.en: The Bodhisattva, prince of five hundred gazelles, is caught in a hunter's net while the whole troop flees - one doe alone stays by him. As the hunter nears she offers her own life first: 'kill me and then the gazelle prince - he is my husband.' Astonished, the hunter answers in verse that he will kill neither, that she shall keep company with her beloved spouse - and leads both away at liberty.
summary.zh: 菩薩生為五百羚之首，誤入獵網，群羚盡逃，唯雌羚相守。獵人將至，雌羚請先殺己：「牠是我的丈夫。」獵人驚異，以偈答「二者皆不殺」，遂放兩羚同去。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The gazelle prince struggled against the net in vain, feet sorely wounded; the doe ran to and fro urging him to exert himself, and when the hunter in brown clothes drew near with bow and arrows she approached him with a courageous heart: 'O hunter, draw thy sword and first kill me, and then kill the gazelle prince - he is my husband.' The hunter replied in verse that he would kill neither: thou shalt keep company with thy beloved spouse; and she answered blessing his own household. His astonishment grew greater still, and he went away leaving both gazelles at liberty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Gazelle and the Hunter (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkeys Saved from Death by Fire

region.en: Tinduka tree by a hill village (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山村鎮杜迦樹（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLII, The Monkeys Saved from Death (Kah-gyur ii. 115-116)

summary.en: Tired of crop-raiding monkeys, the villagers cut down every tree but one Tinduka, ringed it with thorns, and set a watchman: when all five hundred monkeys climb the ripe tree they are to be killed. Panic seizes the troop; the chief alone sits calm - 'the busy and the idle are like unto each other.' But a good monkey frees a young captive in the village, who sets the whole place on fire; the villagers rush home to fight the blaze, and the monkeys come down and escape.
summary.zh: 村民厭猴食禾，伐盡周圍之樹，只留一株鎮杜迦，四周設棘篱並派守望者，待猴群盡上樹便聚殲。眾猴驚惶亂竄，猴王靜坐誦偈；而村中一隻被囚幼猴被善猴放脫後縱火焚村，村人奔救，猴群趁機下樹逃脫。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: When the Tinduka tree had put forth ripe flowers and fruits, all five hundred monkeys climbed it, the watchman reported, and the villagers came armed with bows, arrows and battle-axes to cut the tree down. Fear came upon the monkeys, who sprang to and fro; the chief sat still, answering their reproach in a verse: the busy and the idle are like unto each other; the ends of the tree are many; let food be taken by him who is intent upon his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Monkeys Saved from Death (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the village a young monkey sat captive, absorbed in thought: the whole troop of the villagers had taken the field to put his relatives to death. A good monkey, finding him, freed him from his bonds - and the young monkey at once set the village on fire. Hearing the clamour, the men cried that a great calamity had occurred while they were far away, hastened home to put out the fire, and the monkeys came down from the Tinduka tree and ran away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Monkeys Saved from Death (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dream of the Caldron: Incredulity Punished

region.en: Hill-town with elephant stables (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 有象廄的山鎮（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLIII, Incredulity Punished (Kah-gyur iv. 246)

summary.en: One monkey-chief dreams he and his five hundred are boiled alive in a caldron, and leads his band away; the other chief scoffs - 'do dreams then turn out true?' - and stays on his wide domain. Later a blazing sheep drives fire into the king's elephant stables, and the doctor prescribes monkeys cooked in barley-meal for the scorched elephants; hunters catch all the monkeys of the neighborhood, and the incredulous chief's band is thrown into the caldron alive.
summary.zh: 一猴王夢見全族被活煮於鑊，遂率眾遷離；另一王譏笑「夢也能應驗？」拒不搬遷。其後一隻著火的羊把火帶進王家象廄，燒傷群象；醫者開方須以大麥粉煮猴肉敷治，獵人捕盡近處猴子——不信者一族果然入了鑊。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: One chief dreamed that he was placed alive in a caldron together with a retinue of five hundred monkeys, lamented till break of day, and warned the other chief to move somewhere else. The other answered incredulously: do dreams then turn out true? I possess a widely extended domain, and I shall not go. The believer led his band away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Incredulity Punished (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: A servant-maid roasting barley in the earth struck a wandering sheep with a fire-brand; the sheep ran blazing into the king's elephant stable, and many elephants were scorched. The doctor prescribed monkeys cooked in barley-meal; hunters caught all the monkeys residing in the neighbourhood, and the doctor threw them alive into the caldron. A deity sang: it is not good to dwell in a town in which discord exists - on account of discord between the sheep and the servant-maid the monkeys perished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Incredulity Punished (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wise and the Foolish Monkey Chiefs

region.en: Hill-village with a kimpaka tree (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 有金波迦樹的山村（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLIV, The Wise and the Foolish Monkey Chiefs (Kah-gyur iv. 247)

summary.en: A kimpaka tree by a hill-village bends to the ground with fruit. The first monkey-chief looks at it and draws his conclusion in a verse: the tree stands near the village, yet the children have not partaken of the fruit - so the fruit is not conducive to enjoyment; he leads his band away. The second chief lets his monkeys feast, and they suffer agonies in consequence.
summary.zh: 山村旁的金波迦樹果實壓枝垂地。第一猴王察樹而誦偈：「樹近村而童子未嘗其果，可知其果不可食。」率眾而去；第二王縱猴飽食，果有劇毒，眾猴痛苦不堪。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: After looking at the tree, the first chief said in a verse: although the tree stands near the village, yet have the children not partaken of the fruit; from that it may be concluded that the fruit of this tree is not conducive to enjoyment. He led his band away; the second leader let his monkeys partake of the fruit, and they suffered agonies in consequence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Wise and the Foolish Monkey Chiefs (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Monkeys and the Moon in the Well

region.en: Well in a moonlit forest (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 林中月下之井（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLV, The Monkeys and the Moon (Kah-gyur iv. 249)

summary.en: Seeing the moon's reflection in a well, a monkey-leader cries that the moon has fallen in and the world is without a moon - must they not draw it out? They form a chain, the first hanging from a branch and each from the tail above; the branch bends, the water is troubled, the reflection vanishes, the branch breaks, and all fall into the well - 'when the foolish have a foolish leader they all go to ruin.'
summary.zh: 猴王見井中月影，驚呼月落井中、天下無月，急須撈起。眾猴結鏈，首猴懸樹枝，依次抓尾；樹枝彎曲，水動影散，枝斷猴墜，盡落井中——「愚者遇愚主，同歸於盡。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; this episode parallels the widely known monkey-and-moon story across Buddhist Asia.

passages.text: The leader said: the moon has fallen into the well; the world is now without a moon; ought not we to draw it out? They formed a chain, the first monkey hanging on to the branch of a tree and each to the tail above; the branch bent a good deal, the water was troubled, the reflection of the moon disappeared, the branch broke, and all the monkeys fell into the well and were disagreeably damaged. A deity sang: when the foolish have a foolish leader, they all go to ruin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Monkeys and the Moon (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Bird assembly of the flamingo-king (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 天鵝王（頻陀羅王）鳥會（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLVI, The Peacock as Bridegroom (Kah-gyur iii. 90)

summary.en: The birds assemble for the flamingo-king Rashtrapala's daughter to choose a husband; she picks the peacock, who straightway expands his tail and dances. Asked why he dances, the birds explain he is to be her husband - and Rashtrapala refuses him: shameless and bold, afflicted with impudence, however lovely his voice and lapis-lazuli neck.
summary.zh: 群鳥齊集為頻陀羅王之女擇婿，公主選中孔雀，孔雀即開屏起舞。王問其故，答曰「他將為婿」，王遂拒婚：「其聲雖美、其頸如琉璃，然輕狂無禮，斷不以此女妻之。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: When she had looked at the peacock she said he should be her husband; on hearing this the peacock expanded his tail and began to dance. Rashtrapala asked why he danced, was told it was because he was to be his daughter's husband, and refused: for he is shameless and bold. Pressed in a sloka about his lovely voice, beautiful colour, wings set with eyes and neck like lapis lazuli, the king repeated the verdict: yet I will not give her to thee, for thou art afflicted with impudence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Peacock as Bridegroom (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Crow with the Golden Cap

region.en: House-roof crow-call (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 屋頂鴉噪（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLVII, The Crow with the Golden Cap (Kah-gyur iv. 221)

summary.en: A crow cries agreeably to a woman whose husband is far away; she vows a golden cap if he returns safe. He does, the crow presents itself, and she pays the promised cap - with which the crow struts about until a falcon, drawn by the gold, tears off its head: 'a possession which has no necessary cause will be taken away.'
summary.zh: 烏鴉向寡居婦人悅鳴，婦人許願夫歸則贈金冠。夫安然歸來，烏鴉討得金冠，戴之飛揚；因金冠招來鷂鷹，啄去其首——「無因而得之物，必遭人奪。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The crow uttered agreeable sounds, and the woman promised a golden cap if her husband returned home safe. He did return, the crow appeared with an eye to the reward, and she gave it the cap; the crow put it on and flew hither and thither - but on account of the golden cap a falcon tore off its head. A deity sang: a possession which has no necessary cause will be taken away; the gold on the crow's head was looked after by a robber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Crow with the Golden Cap (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Revengeful Crow and the Rishi's Silence

region.en: Rishi's park at Rajagriha (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王舍城仙園（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLVIII, The Revengeful Crow (Kah-gyur iv. 231)

summary.en: At Rajagriha a hermaphrodite's corpse, fitting neither of the two sex-segregated cemeteries, is laid by a ricinus shrub; a jackal and a crow flatter each other in verses while sharing the feast. The nearby Rishi rebukes the crow for nestling in the shadow of the most wretched of trees devouring the most wretched of corpses; the crow answers with a counter-verse and, enraged, breaks every pot in his kitchen. The Rishi's punishment is silence: never again a word to her, whether for praise or blame - the wise obtain repose only by keeping silence.
summary.zh: 王舍城雌雄同體者死後兩處墓地皆不容，屍身置於蓖麻樹旁；豺與鴉互以偈語諂媚，共享盛宴。鄰近仙人斥鴉於最劣之樹蔭下啄最劣之屍，鴉以反偈回敬，怒而搗毀仙人的廚房器皿。仙人的懲罰是沉默：從此無論毀譽，不再對她說一個字——智者唯以靜默得安。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; the text's talk of a hermaphrodite's corpse reflects ancient Indian burial categories, reported factually.

passages.text: The crow sang the jackal's praises to get a share of the corpse, and he answered in kind; the Rishi saw the pair feeding and cried out that from afar he had seen her, shamelessly nestling in the shadow of the most wretched of trees and devouring the most wretched of corpses. The crow indignantly answered: what is it to this baldpate that the lion and the peacock, feeding on excellent flesh, prolong their existence by means of strangers' gifts? The Rishi retorted: see here the union of the shameless - the most wretched of birds the crow, of beasts the jackal, of trees the ricinus, of men the hermaphrodite, of fields the three-cornered one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Revengeful Crow (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Exceeding great anger sprang up in the crow, and she flew to the Rishi's kitchen, saw nothing there, broke the pots and pitchers, and flew away. Finding the wreckage, the Rishi knew the bad crow had done it, and pronounced his sentence in a verse: to her who has with shameless malice broken the things in the kitchen, in future, whether for praise or for blame, not even the smallest word shall be spoken - the wise ever obtain repose only by keeping silence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Revengeful Crow (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The United Pheasants: One Body, Two Wills

region.zh: 迦波羅洲海岸（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XLIX, The United Pheasants (Kah-gyur iv. 232-233)

summary.en: Two pheasants grow together in one body: Dharmika (Righteous) and Adharmika (Unrighteous). Dharmika, awake first, finds an amrita fruit washed ashore and eats it without waking his partner, reasoning the shared body is nourished either way; Adharmika, offended, bides his time and, waking next, eats a poisonous fruit - both birds fall insensible. Dying, each pronounces a vow: the one to show kindness wherever reborn, the other to be the slayer's antagonist.
summary.zh: 雙雉共體而生：一名法行，一名非法行。法行先醒，得海上漂來的甘露果，念及共用一體便獨食之；非法行懷恨伺機，醒後吞下毒果，二鳥俱昏。臨終各發誓願：一願來生以慈相報，一願來生為仇相殺。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; a Buddhist parallel to the Mundaka Upanishad's two birds on one tree, noted by Schiefner.

passages.text: While Adharmika slept, Dharmika saw an amrita fruit driven ashore and took it out; reflecting that if he ate it the body they shared in common would be nourished, he did not wake the other. When Adharmika awoke and perceived the smell on his partner's breath, he learned the truth and said: as you have not acted rightly therein, I also will bide my time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The United Pheasants (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: On another occasion Adharmika, awake while Dharmika slept, perceived a poisonous fruit the waves had brought ashore and ate it; both birds became insensible. Dying, Adharmika vowed that wherever he might be born again he would be the slayer's antagonist, and Dharmika vowed that wherever he might be born again he would show kindness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The United Pheasants (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Yavana land and the courts of Madhyadesa (symbolic pin at Mathura)
region.zh: 耶婆那之地與中印度諸宮（以馬土臘為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. L, Three Tales about Artists (Kah-gyur ii. 283-285)

summary.en: An ivory carver's grains of 'rice' will not cook - the painter's wife boils them all day; the painter sends him for water to a pond he has merely painted, dead dog beside it, and the carver smashes his jug on the picture. The painter, guesting with a mechanician, seizes the artificial maiden sent to wait on him and she collapses into chips; he then paints himself 'hanged' on the door and lets the mechanician summon the king's men to cut down a corpse that turns out to be a plank. Finally two painters compete on facing walls - one paints a picture, the other drapes his wall in such mosaic that the king declares it the finer 'painting'.
summary.zh: 象牙雕米煮不熟；畫師誘雕匠至畫中死犬之「池塘」取水，碰碎水罐。畫師留宿機械師家，握住機關少女之手，她散作一堆木片；畫師便在門上畫己「自縊」，誘機械師請王官來驗「屍」，斧落方知是門板。最後兩畫師隔簾比藝：一畫壁畫，一以鑲嵌充畫，王誤以其「畫」最妙。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The ivory carver, lodging with a painter, asked the painter's wife to cook the grains of rice he had carved; her wood ran out and the rice stayed raw, and when the painter returned he recognized carved ivory and sent the guest for fresh water to a pond hard by - which he had painted, with a dead dog's body beside it. The carver held his nose at the 'corpse', smashed his jug, and knew he had been fooled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Three Tales about Artists (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: To wait upon the wearied traveller the mechanician sent an artificial maiden he had framed; she washed the painter's feet and stood still. Believing she was sent for his enjoyment, he seized her by the hand to draw her towards him, whereupon she collapsed and turned into a heap of chips. Befooled, he painted his own likeness on the door as if he had hanged himself and hid behind it; the mechanician, finding the maiden in chips and the 'corpse' at the door, summoned the king's officials to inspect the body - and their axe met nothing but a door. The painter came forth: you made a fool of me in private, but I have made a fool of you in the midst of the royal retinue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Three Tales about Artists (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Two painters, each claiming superiority, were set by the king to decorate opposite walls of the entrance hall behind a curtain. In six months one completed a picture; the other covered his wall with mosaic. Admiring the picture, the king was led next door, saw several figures standing well out, and marvelled that this was the more excellent painting - whereupon the artist drew back the curtain and confessed it was no painting at all. The king's astonishment redoubled: this one is the best artist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Three Tales about Artists (1882); not verbatim.
